body: How sets sit next to each other along an aisle. The store-layout view of the same idea as **aisle sequence**.
The sign hanging over each aisle listing the commodities found in it. Two styles, both filled with verbiage inserts selected by which commodities have the most footage.
Collectively, the aisle markers and outriggers that get a customer from the main aisle to a specific set.
Pairing a DSL tag to its shelf position: open the DSL app, scan the tag, scan the shelf strip, confirm *Matched Successfully*, move on. Don't stand there watching it.
The stockroom and receiving area. Where the receiver works and where new-item stock comes from.
A printed card hung from a peg hook when the product is out of stock. Carries the facings, SKU, and description so the peg keeps its place.
Product that won't fit on the shelf. It goes to top stock, onto a **U-boat**, or into **banana boxes** — never left sitting in the aisle. See Part II, Storage.
The cardboard compactor in the back room. You must be 18 or older and be shown that specific machine before operating it.
The container we use for backstock, first choice and near enough the only one. Sturdy, stackable, lidded, and sized so a loaded one is still liftable. From produce or the receiver.
The bottom shelf of a bay. Sits on the shoe and has no prongs, which is what makes it different from an upper.
Each 4-foot segment of a gondola. Occasionally 3 feet depending on the store. Bays are numbered left to right within a commodity.
A rapid rollout of a product or planogram across a whole area at once, usually timed to an ad date.
A section of pegboard extended away from the gondola so pegged product is easier to reach. Three components: bars, brackets, pegboard. Also called an extended pegboard.
A Fred Meyer system the store uses to sign work out. Retail Odyssey associates have no access and are not permitted to sign out work in them.
The top shelf on an endcap, in the promo aisle, or in the grocery lobby. Used for signage and seasonal décor only, not product.
Product placed flat, either underneath upright product in frozen or stacked on top of faced product elsewhere.
Customer Choice Checklane Reinvention. The checklane plan that weights product selection toward natural candy and snacks.
The non-perishable departments: grocery, frozen, dairy, drug/GM, beer and wine. As opposed to the perishable perimeter.
The indented front edge of a shelf, where the data skin mounts. See **data skin**.
Another name for a data skin, from the channel it sits in. See **data skin**.
A bunker or open freezer well. Counted differently from a shelf — see Section 7.10.
Clear plastic mounted to a shelf to stop items sliding off. Attaches with plastic "Christmas tree" clips.
A thin plastic or metal strip with hooks down one side, hung to merchandise product outside its normal set.
See **set**.
The same product merchandised in more than one place in the store — batteries in electronics and at the checklane.
Adding a new item into an existing planogram without rebuilding the set. What a partial project usually involves in a category without strips.
Items whose packaging or contents are compromised: torn boxes, cut bags, smashed cans, leaking cartons. Not sellable. Comes off the set into a labeled box and goes to the receiver.

The clear plastic channel guide that snaps onto the front edge of a shelf and holds the strip. **This is the term we use.** You will also hear *channel*, *data channel*, and *channel strip* — all the same part. Correcting data skins is part of NII and DI work.

**A different job, not yours.** A separate team audits secondary locations of product against the marketing plan, store by store, on a weekly cycle. It's Retail Odyssey work but it isn't Kompass work — nothing in a DC scan touches your reset, and nothing in your reset feeds a DC scan.
Drug / General Merchandise. Covers HBC, OTC, and general merchandise.
Discontinued item. Flagged in the Kompass Notes and marked on the shelf with a closeout tag. Comes off the set and goes to the store associate or into a labeled box.

Clearing a DSL tag at the end of a set so it stops displaying a price. Open the app, select Disassociate, scan, confirm, and the tag goes back on the Kompass cart. **Every leftover tag gets cleared** — an active tag on an empty space is advertising a price for nothing.

Printed in red in small type on the shelf strip: how far that shelf sits above the base shelf. An independent check on shelf heights, taken from a fixed datum rather than measured up the bay. See Section 7.3.
See **damaged product**. The term the acquired companies use.
Plastic insert mounted to a shelf to separate facings and keep items that don't stack well organized.
Direct Store Delivery. Product the vendor orders, delivers, and stocks themselves — Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Frito-Lay. Not ordered or stocked by Kroger, and generally not yours to work.
**Two names for one thing, and you'll see both in the same shift.**
The app on the Zebra used to associate and disassociate tags.

When the product isn't in stock, a same-size item turned **backwards** on the shelf to hold the space open. The hole stays the right width, and whoever fills it later doesn't have to re-measure. Backwards is the point — nobody buys it by mistake.
The date a planogram goes live in the store. Not the date it was created and not necessarily the date you work it.
A 3- or 4-foot section at the end of a gondola, used for seasonal, temporary, or promotional product.
The number of one product placed side by side across the front of a shelf. Shown as **Fac** on the planogram position table and on the strip. Facings are horizontal only — depth is separate.
A two-prong peg hook. Some are two-part for easy removal.
Acrylic or metal rail on the shelf front that keeps product from sliding off. Same job as clearview.
Where your schedule, store assignment, lead's name, and special instructions live. prod.sasretail.com/en/field.
Any furnishing that holds merchandise: gondolas, pegboards, pushers, cases.
Meat, seafood, deli, bakery, produce. Found around the perimeter of the store.

The plastic clip that seats into a pegboard and holds the peg hook. Named for its shape — the two legs and body look like a frog sitting on a table. It occupies **two holes**, and **the left leg goes into the hole specified.** See Part II, Special Fixtures.
The manned checklanes, self-checkouts, and service desk.
**This means two different things, and context tells you which.**
A complete rebuild of a category to a new planogram. See Section 8.
General Merchandise. Non-food items.
The shelving unit that holds the shelves — the main structure of an aisle, secured to the floor. Also called a **run**.
The loading dock at the back of the store where trucks unload. Usually how you get in — through the **man door** beside the dock, not the dock itself. Your lead will confirm.
Health and Beauty Care. Non-medicinal personal care: body wash, soap, shampoo, conditioner, toothpaste, mouthwash.
Plastic device placed on a peg hook behind the product, limiting how many items fit on the peg and holding the product forward.
A J-shaped hook mounted on a shelf, used for impulse product.
A clip-on data skin, one of the holders you'll meet on a DSL set.
Kroger's operating standards, including stock rotation.
Kroger Optimization Management Plan Aligning Store Sales. The program that keeps shelf sets current and aligned to plan. It's the job.
The store's staging cart holding new items, Notes, planograms, strips, and tags for the visit.
The store's designated contact for the visit, typically the Operations Assistant Store Manager. Rarely staffed in practice; the Food Manager often stands in.
The Fred Meyer system where the store signs work out. Store access only.
The weekly instructions for what's changing at this store, including which items are discontinued.
The manufacturer of the ESL rails and holders. Their part numbers are what you order by.
Kroger Personal Finance. Gift cards and telecom.
Layout & Mapping Center of Excellence. The team that maps planograms onto each store's floorplan, deciding which plan lands on which fixture.
The first product a customer sees coming from the main aisle. Planograms carry lead-in indicators showing which end of the set faces the main aisle.

A peg merchandising system that mounts straight to the gondola uprights, with hooks hanging off the bar instead of a pegboard. **The bar is stamped FRONT AND UP, and that stamp is the mechanism, not a label** — the hook's shank and the bar's slots are both D-shaped, and the flats only meet when the bar is the right way up. Wrong way up, the hook rests in the slot without locking. Rated to 150 lbs. See Part II, Special Fixtures.
A partial project correcting or updating part of a set.
The normal person-sized door beside a loading dock. Drivers use it, and so do we. See **grocery receiving door**.
The planograms assigned to a particular store.
New Item Introduction. A partial project adding new products to an existing set.
Items no longer carried at that store. Either marked down for clearance or returned to the DSD vendor. Comes off the set.
Out of stock. Item not available for sale.
Over-the-Counter. Medicinal items: pain relief, first aid, vitamins and supplements.
Product past its sell-by or expiration date. Comes off the set.
In-aisle signage mounted to the gondola identifying a specific set. Four styles depending on department and fixture type.
Product left over once the shelf is set to plan. Goes to the designated associate or into labeled overstock boxes.
The short label on a shelf part, like H-1, J-3, or O-2. Use it to call a part out loud; use the **Part ID** to actually get one.
The six-digit number you order or request a shelf part by. Always order by Part ID, never by code — one part can carry two different codes.
Planogram Center of Excellence. The central team that builds the planograms. One plan, a whole division.
Metal or plastic hook fitted into a pegboard or grid to hang product.

Perforated board used to hang peg hooks. **The holes are exactly one inch apart, center to center, both across and down.** That turns counting into measuring: a peg three holes over is three inches over, and a tape measure will find it faster than your eyes will.
Person in Charge. The store associate running the building at that moment. Overnight, that is who your lead goes to when a manager isn't on site.
Storage trailers holding construction materials and remodel equipment. Remodel work, not weekly Kompass.
The schematic showing exactly what product goes where, in what quantity. Also called a schematic. The authority for every set you build.
Shelves between hip and eye level. The most valuable space on the gondola, which is why the plan puts specific items there.

The store associate who produces and corrects price tags. **This is the term we use.** The same person is also called the scan coordinator or pricing coordinator — one role, three names. A position you couldn't tag goes to your lead, and your lead takes it to them.
A store's own brand. At Fred Meyer, **Our Brand**.
Two senses, both about height: the overall height of a gondola, and the distance from one shelf to the next. *"Set it to the right profile"* means get the shelf heights right.
Also called the seasonal aisle. Product rotates by season or holiday.
Spring-loaded fixture keeping product pushed to the front of the shelf. Three components: rail, pusher/divider, end pieces.

**Two different parts share this word.** A **pusher rail** is the plastic track on the shelf front that pushers and end pieces lock into. An **ESL rail** is the clip-in or clip-over channel that holds a digital shelf label. They sit in the same place on the shelf and do completely different jobs.

Fred Meyer's title for the person leading a remodel or relay overnight. Same role Kroger elsewhere calls a Remodel Team Leader. Not part of your escalation path — day-of issues go to your Team Lead, then to me.
An overhaul of a shelf to rearrange product or bring it back to planogram.
A major change to an existing planogram — a section, a department, or a whole store.
The technical name of the app you clock in and out on. Also called the **SAS Retail App**, and in conversation just the Field App. Same tool, three names.
Shelving above the shoppable part of a gondola. Another name for the **top stock** shelf. Third name for the same shelf, so it's here to be looked up, not taught.
Remodel Operations Manager. Kroger's person in charge of a remodel project. Not part of your escalation path.
Older product to the front, newer product to the back of each facing. Not optional, and invisible to anyone walking the finished set.
Remodel Team Leader. Kroger's title for the person leading a remodel overnight. At Fred Meyer this role is the **Relay Manager**. Not part of your escalation path.
See **gondola**.
See **POG**.
Self-Checkout. Also called USCAN.
See **promo aisle**.

The order sets are laid out along an aisle. Your planogram sits in that order, which is why a set that appears to be in the wrong place is usually a sequence question, not a planogram error. The word is also used on remodels for the order resets and moves get completed.
A grouping of like items: pickles, peanut butter, laundry detergent. Also called a **commodity**.
The size field in a planogram code. **F** is feet, **D** is doors, **I** is inches. A frozen set reading D05 is five doors, not five feet. See Section 7.1.
A 7-inch metal extender used to sit a name-brand item next to Our Brand for comparison. Carries its own commodity code, 000.
A small sign calling out a sale, feature, or price.
When a product can't go on or come off a shelf because the shelf above is in the way. Usually means a height is wrong.
The support the gondola is built on. Extends from the gondola along the floor and carries the base shelf.
Stock Keeping Unit. The retailer's number for a specific product, size, and variety. One SKU can have more than one facing.
Plastic sleeves product sits inside to stay straight and organized. Used in specific dairy sets, canned cat food, and cake décor.

The symbol printed on a shelf strip when an item carries on into the next bay. It continues on the **same shelf number, at the same height** — the same horizontal row, so look sideways rather than up or down. The facing count on the strip is the **total across both bays**, not the part in front of you. See Section 7.7.
**This means two different things, and context tells you which.**

Formerly Rebotics. A verification tool that pairs AI with our planograms to confirm a set was completed correctly. It reads the section photos. Where photographing is part of your role, you submit in the app yourself and it tells you what needs addressing before you leave the aisle. See Section 9.5.

The printed strip that slides into the data skin. Carries product placement, facing count, stack height, and POG data. In a DSL store it also carries the **tag size**, and it's what you scan to associate a tag.
A fixture inside another fixture. It inherits the parent's number and takes a three- or four-digit code: 203 is the third sub-fixture on fixture 2. See Section 7.10.
Extra reset work created by a new-item initiative. The reason a partial gets bigger than the notes suggested.
Store Within a Store. Enclosed areas in high-theft locations holding cosmetics, infant formula, laundry detergent, and similar.
A style of outrigger used in OTC.

The price label for one product, placed to the left of the product it belongs to. Technically a **UPL**. In a converted store the paper tag is replaced by a **DSL**; in a store that hasn't converted yet, the paper tag is still the tag. Check which kind of store you're in before you start.
The merchandised portion of a manned checklane. Sized Medium, Large, or XL.

An old name for the store's handheld ordering and inventory unit, sometimes heard as *Telson*. The hardware line passed through Symbol and Motorola and ended up with **Zebra**, so the device in a store associate's hand today is a Zebra. If someone says Telxon, they mean the Zebra.
Overstock stored on the shelf above a set, and the name of that shelf. Maximum three high, above the matching set, labels forward, no heavy items.
Slides into the slot behind the channel data strip. Unchanged by the DSL rollout — the slot is still there.
The green six-wheeled cart, narrow and U-shaped in profile, that Fred Meyer uses for vendor stock and backstock. Always walked, never ridden or coasted.
Unit of Measure.
Universal Product Code. The barcode. When the description and the UPC disagree, **scan the UPC** — descriptions are abbreviated and repeat across similar items.
Unit Price Label. The technical name for a paper price tag — the label carrying the item price and the per-unit price. If you hear UPL on a call or in a report, it means the paper tag, not a DSL.
Any shelf with prongs on the back that insert into the gondola. Different from a base shelf.
A company providing merchandise or service to a store. Includes us.
The weekly FedEx shipment holding planograms, strips, and tags.
A display flanking an endcap. The 3-tier basket hung on an endcap side is a wing.

The store's handheld scanner. Zebra Technologies absorbed the old **Telxon** and Symbol hardware lines, so anything anyone calls a Telxon or Telson is one of these. Used with the DSL app to associate and disassociate tags. It belongs to the store, not to us. **Leads: ask for it early AM, before the shift starts. No Zebra by mid-shift, escalate — don't wait it out.** I provide the login.
